about: Giovanni Mesina calls himself “the shepherd who makes wine.” His family raised sheep for three generations in the mountainous Barbagia of Sardinia, and he came to Umbria as a child in the 1960s. He still keeps a flock of around a thousand sheep, selling the milk to a local cooperative, and farms vines among orchards, woods and olive groves in the hills of Pianello, northeast of Perugia. He bottled his first vintage in 2017 from about three hectares.

Vermentino is rare in landlocked Umbria; Giovanni planted it as a nod to his Sardinian roots. The vines grow at around 300 metres on marl and limestone, and are farmed organically. His winemaking is hands-off: wild-yeast fermentation, stainless steel tanks, no fining or filtration and no added sulfites. Vermentuzzo spends a couple of days on its skins, which gives it a pale amber tint and a little extra texture.

Despite its inland origin, Vermentuzzo is often described as saline and almost coastal, with honeysuckle, grapefruit and thyme alongside stone fruit, citrus peel and wild herbs. Its bright acidity makes it a lively match for grilled shrimp, scallops or anything with herbs and lemon. Like all of Giovanni’s wines, it is made in tiny quantities, and the name is a playful twist on the grape, in the same spirit as his Trebbiozzo and Ciliegiozzo.
facts: About two days of skin contact; wild-yeast fermentation
Organic, about 300 m elevation, marl and limestone
